doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Charlie Parker as master compiler and the Desmond interview
summary: Parker's quotes in rhythm changes, and a Parker interview with Paul Desmond.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: I just — a gift from God. I don’t know what else to say. And I never have to use it because I tell people, when I listen to Art Tatum, the only album I ever owned by him was “Piano Begins Here.” And I say it should be called “Piano Begins Here and Ends Here.” You know. I’m joking. But I don’t think there’s ever been a piano player like him. I mean Oscar Peterson is close. But for me, sometimes now he plays too many notes, both of them. I can’t do it, I’m just saying, my point with the students is if you heard me and were knocked out by my piano playing, or Herbie Hancock or anybody, and they kept playing sixteenth notes all the time, to me it’d get boring. You need variety. So [scats] or patterns [scats]. There’s any and everything goes. I mean go back to the classical composers. And I say this. Look as much as I love Charlie Parker, I’m not, what’s the word, a jazz historian. I can’t talk about the history too much, only the people I loved and some stories I heard but I can’t talk about their life and I don’t plan to. But Charlie Parker to me may be the greatest improviser of his day and he influenced everybody on all instruments, not to negate Art Tatum, but he to me was a master compiler. It was very interesting, I thought about this, because he took all the tunes of the day and all the classical he heard, and whatever other kind of music he heard, and he was a genius, incredible ear. I’m sure he had perfect pitch, but whatever. And he was able to © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

pick all these little things and play them in any key and put them together, like Ella Fitzgerald and Mel Torme a little bit. Maybe not as much as Bird you know. And that was the thing of the day. Sonny Stitt and a couple of people, they would play, you know, whatever it is, a classical piece [scats] I don’t know what the piece that was, but Sonny Stitt plays that. But Bird would, and I noticed Charlie Parker, I only noticed this about eight years ago, on rhythm changes, the first eight bars of rhythm changes, usually in the key of G on alto, he would make a quote from a famous piece, jazz or classical. You know [scats]. Humoresque, but he put it doing this tempo, and he’d [scats] you know he’d jazz it up and it was incredible. Then he’d play his licks after that and dovetail it together. You know. It would go on — [microphone displaced] Ooh I dropped this

And I was saying he was a master compiler I think. I loved watching his interview with Paul Desmond. There’s something that really touched my heart, for whatever he was with the drugs and everything. And you know Desmond is saying, “You’ve gone way beyond all of us.” And he said, “Well I practice ten hours a day.” But he didn’t practice ten hours a day for twenty years. It was only a few years. He died at 35 or whatever. But he said, and he said it very graciously with a little smile on his face if you look at that video, he says, “I just try to give the people something for the people.” And I said wow, that’s so beautiful. And he’s just playing so melodic, and of course he played a lot of fast stuff. He wasn’t showing off. And then he’d just play a little phrase with some vibrato and it melts your heart. So he had everything. You know? And so getting back to a little of what I was mentioning before, for me, I had a fake book, the original brown fake book with hundreds of tunes in it, spiral bound, and I used to play it with a friend of mine named Hugh Young and me, we used to play clarinet duets. We’d get together and we’d go [scats]. He’d play that and because I knew chords a little better than my friend, he had a much better ear and much better sound, which I never got a great sound on clarinet. And he improvised a little better. He used to play with the Lawrence Welk Show when Pete Fountain came on. I couldn’t do that yet. His dad was real proud. He was only 13, I was 14.
